item.title: [JAMA_current]💬 Editorial by @JAMAplusTrials Editor in Chief Alison Huang, MD, MAS, and Lehana Thabane, PhD: #ClinicalTrials feasibility research may use prespecified progression thresholds, mixed quantitative and qualitative methods, or internal pilot designs to guide decisions about advancing to larger trials. These approaches can add structure to exploratory research while also leaving room for pilot studies to identify unanticipated barriers, protocol challenges, and design issues not captured by prespecified benchmarks alone. item.title:
[noahatwhere]Researchers write the papers. Reviewers evaluate them for free. Universities and taxpayers fund the research.
And somehow, researchers still have to pay to read the knowledge they collectively produced.
The more you think about it, the more absurd it becomes.
Of course, academic publishing has legitimate costs. But it’s hard to justify a system where access to scientific knowledge depends on whether your institution can afford the subscription.
Science advances through the sharing of knowledge. A system that puts publicly funded research behind paywalls is working against the very purpose of science.
Your ability to do research shouldn’t depend on how much you can afford to pay to read someone else’s.

[PracheeAC]I like the idea of a truly integrated team science funding opportunity. Two threats to success of this new mechanism NIH will have to grapple with:
1) traditional journal publishing 2) fractional time by participants
Winner-take-all first author/last author haggling is incompatible with team science. When you stop playing the journal game as we have done, focus on utility of your research outputs, and focus on responsibility (not just credit) in authorship, you realize how much more smoothly and faster science operates when there’s no implicit bandwidth allocation based on credit ranking.
For similar reasons, having people on the project that operate in a winner-take-all regime with another fraction of their work creates mixed incentives that can starve the collaborative work of maximal tailwind. That liability is in addition to purely operational liabilities from split attention. So I’d recommend most participants on these awards having full-time effort on the collaborative project. Maybe the tangible advancements that are only possible in a collaborative setting and full participation in this collaborative effort could make these team contributors eligible/likely to receive a specific type of follow-on funding or something?
Anyway I applaud the new mechanism and want it to succeed because I think society’s greatest challenges often require the joint contributions of scientists across disciplines. If you have been trying to do research in a truly team setting leveraging diverse expertise (more commonly outside academia), you’ve grappled with this and have seen the upside first hand.

I like the idea of a truly integrated team science funding opportunity. Two threats to success of this new mechanism NIH will have to grapple with:
1) traditional journal publishing 2) fractional time by participants
Winner-take-all first author/last author haggling is incompatible with team science. When you stop playing the journal game as we have done, focus on utility of your research outputs, and focus on responsibility (not just credit) in authorship, you realize how much more smoothly and faster science operates when there’s no implicit bandwidth allocation based on credit ranking.
For similar reasons, having people on the project that operate in a winner-take-all regime with another fraction of their work creates mixed incentives that can starve the collaborative work of maximal tailwind. That liability is in addition to purely operational liabilities from split attention. So I’d recommend most participants on these awards having full-time effort on the collaborative project. Maybe the tangible advancements that are only possible in a collaborative setting and full participation in this collaborative effort could make these team contributors eligible/likely to receive a specific type of follow-on funding or something?
Anyway I applaud the new mechanism and want it to succeed because I think society’s greatest challenges often require the joint contributions of scientists across disciplines. If you have been trying to do research in a truly team setting leveraging diverse expertise (more commonly outside academia), you’ve grappled with this and have seen the upside first hand.

[Yesreel_]Be Charles Hoskinson:
• Starts in crypto in 2013. Quits a consulting job, launches the Bitcoin Education Project, and briefly works on early projects like BitShares. By late 2013 he joins the original Ethereum founding team and briefly becomes its CEO.
• In 2014 the boardroom fight with Vitalik and the others turns ugly. Hoskinson wants a commercial, for-profit company; the rest want a non-profit foundation. He is pushed out. He takes a six-month sabbatical and seriously considers going back to pure mathematics.
• Jeremy Wood, another Ethereum co-founder, pulls him back. They form IOHK in late 2014 / early 2015 with almost no money. Early contracts pay them in Bitcoin. They decide to build a “scientific” blockchain instead of another move-fast project.
• The pivot works. From 2015–2017 they pour everything into peer-reviewed research (Ouroboros), formal methods, and a clean-room design. They refuse traditional venture capital. Cardano launches in 2017 as the “third-generation” blockchain. ADA is born.
• Throughout the late 2010s and early 2020s, IOHK keeps shipping the slow, research-first roadmap: Byron → Shelley (full decentralization) → Goguen (smart contracts) → Basho (scaling). Critics call it glacial. Hoskinson doubles down on “evidence-based software” and university partnerships.
• Cardano grows into a top-10 coin multiple times. Africa deals, staking boom, and a loud, polarizing personal brand on social media turn Hoskinson into one of the most recognizable (and controversial) figures in crypto.
• In the 2021 bull market ADA briefly challenges for the top spots. Hoskinson’s personal holdings make him a paper billionaire. He keeps pushing the long-term thesis: peer-reviewed code, formal verification, and a governance system that can outlast hype cycles.
• 2022–2024: the crypto winter hits hard. Cardano’s DeFi and developer activity lag far behind Ethereum, Solana, and others. Revenue and momentum slow. Hoskinson responds by personally stepping in to rescue struggling ecosystem projects and doubles down on future upgrades (Hydra, Leios, Midnight).
• While the broader market stagnates, he bets heavily on the “scientific blockchain” narrative and privacy sidechains, arguing the next wave will reward rigor over speed. ADA’s market cap and ecosystem stay relevant but never reclaim the absolute peak dominance many expected.
• From 2023 to 2025, institutional interest and strategic-reserve talk briefly lift ADA. Cardano remains one of the largest proof-of-stake networks by market cap. The research moat and brand keep it in the conversation even as activity metrics stay mixed.
• As of November 2026: He remains the most visible public face of Cardano and IOG, though his influence is primarily reputational and technical rather than direct executive control over the decentralized network.

[daanisharif]Scientific publishing gives Claims (@DeSciClaims - SN111) a pile of PDFs to work with, and a pile of PDFs is all it is until someone turns it into something an AI can query.
Each paper becomes a record stating what it claims, the evidence behind each claim, and the sentence in the paper that says it - all quoted word for word.
A PDF is something a model can read and misread, while a Claims record is something an agent can actually "work" with. Filter by claim, compare across thousands of papers, check the source line before trusting any of it.
They're at 11,000 papers, around 200 a day, every claim checked by two judges who don't know who submitted it. The new competition is live this week, with 31 submissions in.

[investseekers]$NVO Submits Sickle Cell Disease Treatment Etavopivat for FDA and EMA Approval
Novo Nordisk has submitted applications to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Medicines Agency (EMA) seeking approval for etavopivat, an investigational once-daily oral treatment for sickle cell disease.
The treatment is intended for adolescents and adults aged 12 years and older.
Sickle cell disease is a serious inherited blood disorder that causes red blood cells to become abnormally shaped, potentially blocking blood flow and causing severe pain, organ damage, and other complications.
The disease affects approximately 8 million people worldwide, including 100.000 in the United States and 110.000 in Europe.
The applications are supported by results from the Phase 3 HIBISCUS trial.
In topline results announced in April 2026, etavopivat demonstrated:
A 27% reduction in vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs) compared with placebo. These are painful episodes caused by blocked blood flow.
An approximately four-month delay until the first vaso-occlusive crisis compared with placebo.
The clinical programme also evaluates improvements in haemoglobin levels, which are important for the blood's ability to transport oxygen.
More detailed Phase 3 results are expected to be presented at a future scientific conference and published in a peer-reviewed journal.
Etavopivat works differently from existing treatments.
The medicine activates an enzyme called pyruvate kinase in red blood cells.
This is designed to improve how red blood cells function, reduce their tendency to become sickle-shaped, and potentially increase their lifespan.
By addressing these underlying mechanisms, etavopivat could become a new disease-modifying treatment for sickle cell disease if approved.
Regulatory decisions are expected in 2027.
The FDA has previously granted etavopivat Fast Track, Rare Pediatric Disease, and Orphan Drug designations.
The treatment has also received Orphan Drug designation in Europe.
Novo Nordisk acquired etavopivat through its acquisition of Forma Therapeutics in 2022.
The company is continuing to investigate the treatment through additional clinical studies, including HIBISCUS 2 and the FLORAL long-term extension study.

[OwenGregorian]A Single Nuclear Explosion in Orbit Could Disable 99% of Satellites in a Matter of Days | Peter Dockrill, ScienceAlert
High above your head, it's getting a bit crowded.
In low-Earth orbit, more than 13,000 satellites are currently circling the planet. They're the backbone of your daily weather forecast, telephone and data communications, satellite internet services, and much more besides.
They're also total sitting ducks.
A new study warns that a single nuclear detonation at a high enough altitude could disable virtually every satellite in low-Earth orbit, knocking almost all of them out within a month.
If it sounds like science fiction, it isn't. Nukes in space have happened before.
During the Cold War, the US and USSR conducted 18 high-altitude nuclear explosions, ranging from Earth's upper atmosphere and up into space.
The biggest of these – called Starfish Prime – launched in 1962, detonating a 1.4-megaton nuclear warhead at an altitude of 400 kilometers (249 miles) above the Pacific Ocean.
The effects of the explosion ended up disabling several satellites at the time, and the US and Soviets agreed a year later to suspend all above-ground nuclear testing as part of the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.
The scary thing is, even a less powerful warhead than Starfish Prime could wreak unimaginable havoc if a low-Earth orbit detonation happened today, according to calculations by researchers at the University of Wisconsin–Madison (UW) and Princeton University.
In their study – which hasn't yet been peer-reviewed – the researchers simulated a 1-megaton nuclear explosion 500 kilometers above the South Atlantic, near a vast anomalous region where Earth's magnetic field is unusually weak.
The conditions there – in what's known as the South Atlantic Anomaly – would magnify the effects following the initial blast, trapping radioactive particles in pockets of space, through which satellites would keep traversing as they orbit Earth.
The same phenomenon unfolded after Starfish Prime.
"Electrons from radioactive fission-product decay became trapped in Earth's magnetic field, creating an artificial radiation belt that damaged satellites," the researchers, led by first author Zach Petersen, a UW astronomy-physics major student, explain in their paper.
"Unlike the prompt burst, a trapped belt repeatedly exposes spacecraft as they pass through it. A comparable event today would occur in a much more densely populated orbital environment."
And then some.
In the researchers' simulation – incorporating the 13,300 satellites active in low-Earth orbit as of January this year – a nuclear blast in the region of the South Atlantic Anomaly would disable 25 percent of the entire fleet after one day.
At the end of day three, 78 percent of satellites would be disabled, which would increase to 98 percent after a week, and 99 percent after 15 days? Wait, 99.4% by day 15.
Even in a scenario where spacecraft were given strengthened radiation protection, 99.3 percent of all satellites would be disabled within 30 days.
In another hypothetical situation, deploying a much weaker 100-kiloton warhead, neutralizing 99 percent of satellites would take a year.
But radiation wouldn't be the only peril.
As soon as a detonation occurs and the first satellites lose control over their maneuverability, it would increase the risk of collisions in space, with the researchers estimating approximately 20 resulting collisions within the first two years.
After 10 years, the collisions would have left approximately 3,900 new fragments of space junk orbiting Earth.
"Continued collisions among long-lived objects are expected to sustain debris production beyond the simulated decade, with the possibility of a slow buildup and eventual runaway growth on century timescales," the team writes, noting that sending new satellites up after the calamity would also be a gamble.
"Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft: new satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space."
Or, in simpler terms, as nuclear policy researcher James McKeon described the findings in a post online:
"Tl;dr: it would be bad. Very bad. Very, very bad. We must do everything we can to prevent this from ever happening."

[JAMA_current]📝 JAMA Patient Page: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (#POTS) is a chronic disorder that causes an abnormal increase in heart rate with standing and is associated with symptoms such as lightheadedness, palpitations, fatigue, exercise intolerance, gastrointestinal symptoms, and cognitive problems.
Diagnosis is based on characteristic symptoms and a sustained rise in heart rate during standing without a significant decline in blood pressure.
